cells.tense: You're standing where things arrive and deciding what is worth keeping, right now, as it comes.
cells.ask: Keep one thing that arrived this week and say out loud what you're letting go so it has room. Do it before the week turns.
cells.core:
Things come to you and you sort them without a lot of drama. Something arrives, you look at what it costs to hold, and you keep it or you don't. That used to take you longer.

There's a fairness running under it that doesn't announce itself. You're not measuring every exchange, but what you give and what comes back has a shape to it, and you notice when it's off. That's why the call goes fast — the answer is already made somewhere before you get to it. What's coming in now isn't asking you to be more careful. It's asking you to feed the thing you want more of, and you get to choose which one that is.
cells.sheetLine: You sort what comes in, and you know when the exchange is off.
cells.verb: sorting what arrives into what gets kept and what gets let go
cells.place: where what's outside is coming in and you decide what to meet

cells.tense: You're already living past this moment, bracing for a future that hasn't written itself yet.
cells.ask: Pick one thing you're holding because of what's coming and let it leave today, on its own, without lining up what replaces it.
cells.core:
You're sorting what hasn't arrived yet. Something shows up and you're already three steps out, keeping what you think you'll need and clearing what you think you won't. It's hard to be in the room with what's actually here when you're standing in the next one.

You're making the call about things that haven't reached you, and one call is landing on top of the next. What's arriving doesn't need you to have already decided. It needs you here when it lands, so you can feel whether it's yours to keep, instead of knowing in advance. That's the whole ask. Nothing gets lost by waiting one beat to find out.
cells.sheetLine: You're deciding about what hasn't arrived yet.
cells.verb: sorting what arrives into what gets kept and what gets let go
cells.place: where what's outside is coming in and you decide what to meet

lint.detail: "already" ×2 in one core — the house voice showing

cells.tense: You're standing at a door you already walked through, still deciding whether to open it.
cells.ask: Name one thing already in your life that you're treating as temporary and give it a place today — a shelf, a day, a standing slot.
cells.core:
What's arriving isn't being met. Things come in and the call gets made late, or it doesn't get made and they pile up. Keeping and letting go have both gone quiet, so whatever shows up just sits there. When this is working you feel the arrival, weigh what it costs to hold, and act on it — sometimes in the same hour. That motion is what's missing.

Going through the motions of keeping things in order isn't the same as making the call. This isn't about feeling more or pushing harder; it's that the reflex to move on something real has stalled. One thing that's genuinely yours to move, moved today, and the current comes back through on its own.
cells.sheetLine: Things arrive and you're not the one deciding.

cells.tense: You're already the one sorting what comes in, and you talk about it like it happens to you.
cells.ask: Say plainly, to one person, that a call about what to keep or drop was yours, and then hold that call instead of reopening it.
cells.core:
You decide what stays. You've been deciding it for a while — what gets kept, what gets let go, what has room and what doesn't. Somewhere along the way it started sounding like circumstances, or other people, or just how things shook out.

You're doing the work while calling it something that happens on its own. That costs you, because a decision you don't own is one you keep re-checking, and the re-checking is the tiredness. Saying one call out loud won't change what you did. It changes who gets credit for it, and that's the person doing the work. Name it once and don't take it back.
cells.sheetLine: You decide what stays. You haven't said so.
